articles.title: The Atlantic Announces Roles for Zachary Fryer-Biggs, Sophie Haigney, Jebediah Reed, Kevin Roose, Lindsey Sitz, Alex Stockton, and Robert F. Worth
articles.summary: Today The Atlantic is announcing seven new roles in the newsroom: Sophie Haigney and Robert F. Worth as staff writers; Zachary Fryer-Biggs, Jebediah Reed, and Alex Stockton as senior editors; Kevin Roose as a contributing writer; and Lindsey Sitz as a producer for video podcasts. Below is the staff announcement from editor in chief Jeffrey Goldberg and executive editor Adrienne LaFrance: Dear everyone, We’re writing to share the exciting news that we’re bringing aboard several excellent journalists. These new colleagues will help us grow The Atlantic and serve our readers, listeners, and viewers. Joining us are Zach Fryer-Biggs, Sophie Haigney, Jeb Reed, Kevin Roose, Lindsey Sitz, and Alex Stockton. We’re also pleased to let you know that a familiar face, our contributing writer Robert F. Worth, is becoming a staff writer. Zach Fryer-Biggs is joining us as a senior editor. He has been an editor and reporter on the national-security beat for more than 15 years, earning a reputation as a champion of aggressive accountability journalism and as a thoughtful, cool-under-pressure colleague even while chasing the most competitive stories of the day. He’s also known for his deep curiosity about all things military. Zach comes to us from CNN, where he served as a supervising editor for national security. Zach has shaped CNN’s coverage of the Iran war, the Pentagon’s boat-strike campaign, and upheaval at the intelligence agencies, among other subjects. Zach was previously the managing editor at Military.com, where he led a news team that earned the Gerald R. Ford Foundation Award for its reporting on recruiting efforts by extremist groups. As a reporter, Zach has covered the Pentagon and intelligence communities for outlets such as Newsweek and the Center for Public Integrity. Sophie Haigney is joining us as a staff writer. She is a fantastically creative and original thinker whose writing has appeared in The New Yorker, The New York Times Magazine, Harper’s, and other publications (including, many years ago, this one ). Most recently she was the web editor for The Paris Review , and wrote a monthly advice column for The Drift . Her first book of essays, Future Relics , is coming next year. Sophie’s work digs deep into everyday phenomena, such as the evolution in how we “search it up” online and the disappearance of the landline from modern fiction. She is the kind of writer who sees things in the world that you can’t believe you didn’t notice yourself—but only once she points them out to you. We’re excited to see her wide array of interests manifest themselves across our reporting. Jeb Reed is joining us as a senior editor, building out our coverage of money and power, among our most important coverage ambitions. Jeb is an extraordinary editor who is drawn to stories that illuminate complex characters, take the reader on a narrative adventure, and often complicate people’s assumptions about how the world works the way it does, and why. He is also skilled at driving incisive, timely coverage of politics, business, technology, and media, qualities that we know will serve him (and Atlantic subscribers) very well. Jeb comes to us from New York magazine, where he has worked since 2013, editing some of the most memorable writers and features published in recent years. Most recently, he served as the editor of Intelligencer . Before that, Jeb did stints at The Week, Radar, and—for those who remember that brief, shining moment when tablets represented the future of publishing— The Daily . We couldn’t be more excited that he is joining us. Kevin Roose is joining us as a contributing writer. Kevin, who comes to us from The New York Times , is among the most creative and ambitious journalists covering technology today. His obsessive curiosity about tech is evident in all that he does—and at times, technology is obsessed right back at him. (Recall the time a chatbot tried to break up his marriage.) In addition to his many years of daily reporting, Kevin is the author of four books—most recently, The AGI Chronicles , an excerpt of which is out today in The Atlantic . And he is a co-host of the podcast Machine Gods alongside Casey Newton. We are glad to count Kevin among the brilliant group of writers whose reporting and thinking will help guide us through this revolutionary moment in tech. Lindsey Sitz is coming onboard as a producer supporting video podcasts. She is a brilliant and resourceful Pulitzer Prize–winning journalist who brings more than 15 years of experience writing, directing, producing, and editing visual stories. Lindsey has a unique eye for video and impressive range—knowing exactly how to produce a story to capture the tone and tenor of the narrative. Her seven years as a video journalist at The Washington Post spanned breaking news, investigative docs, and a 10-part docuseries that earned her a Ben Bradlee Award for Courage in Journalism and recognition from the Webby Awards. More recently, as an independent producer, she has worked with Vox Media, National Geographic Society, and Virginia Public Media. We can’t wait to see what she achieves here at The Atlantic . Alex Stockton is joining us as a senior editor focused on growing our video offerings. As we continue to expand in the realms of social video and video podcasts, Alex will help us carve out a new lane for even more video journalism—including working directly with reporters on field reporting, experimenting with new forms such as livestreams, and producing other original videos such as essays and debates. Alex is immensely talented. He has many ambitious ideas, great taste, and an extremely impressive record of telling hard-to-get stories at the highest level. He comes to us from The New York Times , where he has worked as a filmmaker producing Opinion video for several years. His work has drawn huge audiences and won numerous awards. In 2021, he was awarded an Emmy for “Heartache in the Hot Zone,” a video dispatch from two New York hospitals overwhelmed by the first wave of the pandemic. In 2023, he received an Emmy for “The Taliban Promised Them Amnesty. Then They Executed Them,” an investigation into Taliban revenge killings since the United States’ withdrawal from Afghanistan. And in 2025, he won his third Emmy for “Two Weeks Inside Gaza’s Ruined Hospitals,” which followed a doctor on a volunteer mission into a war zone. Previously, Alex created hybrid-format video journalism at Vice News Tonight on HBO. Robert F. Worth is joining us as a staff writer. Bobby has been a prolific Atlantic contributing writer since 2023, covering a wide array of stories from around the country and the world. He has profiled Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, dug into the assassination of Shinzo Abe in Japan, surveyed the new Syria shortly after the fall of Bashar al-Assad, and reported from conflict zones in the Middle East, Ukraine—and, last winter, the Upper Midwest . He’s just back from Cuba, currently in Sicily, and actively watching developments in Yemen. Bobby is the very definition of game , and there is no story or region too intimidating for him. When you send Bobby somewhere—wherever it is—you know that he will come back with extraordinary details, ground-level clarity, and a story that demonstrates to the reader that there is simply no substitute for reporting about a place from the place itself. Bobby wrote his first Atlantic story in 1995—a profile of a model prison in Pennsylvania, edited by Jack Beatty. At the time he was an aspiring journalist, struggling to escape graduate school. During his decades away from the magazine, he did stints as a freelance book reviewer, a crime reporter in New York (where he was born and raised), a foreign correspondent for The New York Times in Baghdad and later Beirut, and a roving international writer for The New York Times Magazine . He also wrote a book, A Rage for Order , about the Arab uprisings and their bloody aftermath, published in 2016. Bobby is physically fearless, boundlessly curious, and based in Washington, D.C. Please join us in welcoming Zach, Sophie, Jeb, Kevin, Lindsey, Alex, and Bobby. Best wishes, Jeff and Adrienne Press Contacts: Anna Bross and Paul Jackson | press@theatlantic.com

articles.title: The Atlantic ’s October Cover: Anne Applebaum on the “Empire of Grift” and the Revolution in American Foreign Policy
articles.summary: In The Atlantic ’s October cover story, “ Empire of Grift ,” staff writer Anne Applebaum examines how far-right ideologues have transformed American foreign policy into a tool of private gain and antidemocratic reaction. Instead of making the world safe for democracy, she writes, U.S. foreign policy is rewiring the international order. Reporting from Brazil, Applebaum reveals that the United States is not the ally Brazilians once knew. No longer is American power deployed solely by trained diplomats and reliable officials, working through state channels; instead, “informal envoys, private companies, online grifters, and hardened ideologues both inside and outside the government matter more. Unlike their predecessors, these people do not talk about spreading democracy, and don’t want to build long-term relationships. They don’t care about America’s reputation. They are deploying the tools of American diplomacy and government for their own purposes, to promote their own business interests or their own ideological goals, because, suddenly, they can .” Though the Trumpists currently in charge of the U.S. federal government are frequently described as “isolationists,” Applebaum argues that that characterization is wrong. Many of these officials “don’t think of themselves as ordinary Republicans who won an election and will temporarily hold power until the next election. Nor are they mere appendages of Trump. They believe they represent something much greater: the vanguard of a movement that will alter not just America, but the world.” Applebaum continues, “Like earlier revolutionaries, they do not believe that their opponents are legitimate rivals … Their enemies are existential, and they are international: super-spreaders of a ‘wokeness’ plague, or proponents of a fictitious ‘censorship-industrial complex,’ or advocates of ‘regulation’ that will hamper American business, or self-hating promoters of ‘mass migration’ who want to drown Western civilization in a sea of brown-faced aliens. To maintain their power and defeat these enemies, the predators, like their Bolshevik counterparts, cannot rely on traditional diplomacy, because they don’t trust its practitioners.” The democratic world that came into being after 1945—a world based not exclusively on law, but on a set of mostly self-imposed restraints—is changing, Applebaum writes. In the post-1945 democratic order, Applebaum observes, “American power was largely derived from alliances that it refrained from exploiting. Long-term relationships were held to be valuable, because you never knew when you might need your allies.” That U.S.-led democratic order was of enormous benefit to this country and to the world: “America helped build eight decades of peace, prosperity, and eventually democracy in Europe and much of Asia, creating markets for U.S. companies and unprecedented support for U.S. power. This world is fast disappearing. Instead, following the president’s lead, different people inside and outside the administration are seizing the revolutionary moment in order to win zero-sum victories. Countries that hang back from this free-for-all know they will suffer. ‘If we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu,’ Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said at Davos earlier this year. He was right.” Anne Applebaum’s “ Empire of Grift ” was published today at TheAtlantic.com. Please reach out with any questions or requests. articles.title: The Atlantic Launches New Weekly Video Podcast, The Permanent Questions With David Brooks
articles.summary: Today The Atlantic is launching The Permanent Questions , a new video podcast hosted by staff writer David Brooks about the fundamental questions of human life that every generation—and every individual—must attempt to answer. In new episodes publishing every Sunday, David will engage thinkers, writers, and artists in conversations about what makes us human, what gives life meaning, and how we can build richer relationships and a more just society. For the first episode , available today, David is joined by Meghan Sullivan, the Wilsey Family College Professor of Philosophy at the University of Notre Dame, to consider what it means to live a good life. In an introduction to the show, David says: “There are a lot of shows about politics and business and health and tech, but there aren’t enough about the really big questions of life.” The podcast builds on David’s decades of writing about political, cultural, moral, and social issues. David joined The Atlantic’ s staff after many years as a contributing writer, and has recently written about the crucial lessons for the Democratic Party; “ The People Who Will Thrive in the AI Age ,” about why people’s relationship to mental effort will differentiate them; how “ History Is Running Backwards ” and why reactionaries are taking over the world; and “ Something Big Is Happening on Campus ,” on how plenty is going wrong in American higher education, but a lot is also going right. The launch of The Permanent Questions is part of a continued surge of audio and video at The Atlantic , which has doubled its number of weekly shows, podcast staff, and audio revenue in the past year. Since 2025, The Atlantic has launched the video podcasts The David Frum Show and Galaxy Brain with Charlie Warzel, and this past summer expanded its flagship show, Radio Atlantic —co-hosted by Hanna Rosin and Adam Harris , with a weekly Monday video episode hosted by Adam. The podcast is produced by The Atlantic and made possible by support from Yale University, where David is also a presidential senior fellow at Yale Jackson School of Global Affairs. Episodes of The Permanent Questions will be released each Sunday. Viewers can subscribe to watch on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel or wherever they get their podcasts. Please reach out with any questions or requests. Press Contacts: Anna Bross and Paul Jackson | The Atlantic press@theatlantic.com

articles.title: Remembering 9/11, 25 Years Later
articles.summary: Editor’s Note: Washington Week With The Atlantic is a partnership between NewsHour Productions, WETA, and The Atlantic airing every Friday on PBS stations nationwide. Check your local listings , watch full episodes here , or listen to the weekly podcast here . It has been 25 years since nearly 3,000 people died in a terror attack on the World Trade Center on September 11. “As far as I’m concerned, we can never talk about them enough,” Jeffrey Goldberg, the editor in chief of The Atlantic , said last night. Panelists on Washington Week With The Atlantic joined him for a discussion about the lives that were lost, and they examined the fallout from one of the most terrifying events in the nation’s history. The Atlantic staff writer Jonathan Lemire was an intern at New York Daily News on 9/11. When he learned of the attacks on the Twin Towers, his editor sent him to nearby hospitals. “The most harrowing image from that day for me was you could look in” at the beds lined up, “and they stayed empty,” he said last night. “There weren’t the survivors that people thought could be rushed and saved.” Joining Goldberg to discuss this and more: Ann Compton, a former White House correspondent for ABC News; Sally Jenkins, a staff writer at The Atlantic ; Lemire, a staff writer at The Atlantic and a co-host of Morning Joe on MS NOW; Graeme Wood, a staff writer at The Atlantic . Watch the full episode here .
